### Prerequisites

We recommend reading the previous text first to enhance comprehension (<htcite0>).

Is Gravity Really a Force?

We began by describing gravity based on our current understanding, but this has not always been the case. In the past, gravity was seen as a force, and using this perspective helps explain certain phenomena on Earth, as we will explore

Konstantino Adamopoulos et al. highlight that various systems in our bodies can be affected by the strength of the gravitational field. Additionally, they discuss how gravity has influenced species evolution, using as an example the arrangement of internal organs in aquatic snakes versus tree-climbing snakes

On the other hand, it’s also possible to consider that there is no "gravity force" per se, and that other forces might produce similar effects. For instance, the acceleration measured on the Earth’s surface is not constant and partly results from internal Earth pressure, leading us to observe an acceleration that could be associated with a force stemming from this internal pressure

source.text: Hu, X., Shum, C.K. & Bevis, M.

text.text:
The Gravitational Field

A gravitational field is an invisible map of gravity around an object. It shows how strongly the object would pull on something placed at each point. You cannot see or touch the field, just as you cannot see the wind, but you can notice what it does. Around Earth, the field points toward the center of the planet. That is why a dropped ball always falls downward, whether you are in Brazil, Egypt, or Japan.

Figure 1: The gravitational field around Earth. The arrows show that the field pulls objects toward the center of the planet.

Every object with mass has its own gravitational field. A bowling ball has a stronger field than a tennis ball, but both are extremely weak compared with Earth's field. Earth's field reaches far into space and keeps the Moon in orbit. The Moon's field also pulls on Earth, and together with the Sun it helps produce the ocean tides ().

Fields are not used only for gravity. Think about the air around us: we cannot see it, but we can feel the wind. A weather report may show high humidity in one place, while the wind blows at a different speed somewhere else. Because these values change from point to point, scientists can describe the whole atmosphere as a huge interconnected field (). The idea can go even further: a field can be imagined as a kind of uniform medium that fills space, still invisible to our eyes (; ).

source.text: Cook, A.H., Faller, J.E., Nordtvedt, K.L.

text.text:
Gravity Inside the Earth

Gravity is not only a force that acts on things standing on the surface. Every piece of Earth pulls on every other piece, so the force also exists inside the planet. Long ago, this self-gravity helped squeeze the young Earth into a round ball. Today it holds the planet together.

Imagine a giant ball of clay. Each part pulls on the other parts, and the whole ball becomes round and tightly packed. Earth works in a similar way with rock and metal. The upper layers press down on the layers below, creating enormous pressure deep inside. That pressure is not gravity itself, but it is caused by the weight of everything above (). If a tunnel could cross Earth, a stone dropped into it would be pulled toward the center; after passing the center, it would slow down and then be pulled back.

source.text: Cook, A.H., Faller, J.E., Nordtvedt, K.L.

text.text:
What Does "g" Mean?

Scientists use the letter g for the acceleration that gravity gives to a falling object near Earth's surface. It is about 9.8 meters per second per second. This means that, without air resistance, a falling object's speed increases by about 9.8 meters per second every second. After one second it is moving at about 9.8 meters per second; after two seconds, about 19.6 meters per second.

But g is not a constant value. It is slightly different from place to place: about 9.78 at the Equator and about 9.83 near the poles. On a high mountain, gravity is a little weaker because you are farther from Earth's center. Underground changes in the density of rock can also make small differences. Even the Sun and the Moon cause tiny changes during the day. On the Moon, the same kind of acceleration is only about 1.6 meters per second per second. So when we say "g is 9.8," we are giving an average for Earth's surface, not a number that is exactly the same everywhere ().

source.text: Cook, A.H., Faller, J.E., Nordtvedt, K.L.
